clue.text: Parsons, say, with nothing under their cassocks, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear tells the solver the clue's phrase is to be spoken and matched by its sound

parts.note: clergy wearing no underwear beneath their robes would be knickerless

explanation.surface: A question about what parsons wear, or fail to wear, beneath their cassocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parsons' looks like clergy, matching the cassocks, but it is the surname of Nicholas Parsons, the British broadcaster who hosted the radio panel game Just a Minute. The sound match is loose, as 'we hear' and the question mark admit.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas is the first name of the broadcaster Nicholas Parsons, so a Parsons, for example, could be called that.

clue.text: It's most unlikely he's an Arab boy

definitions.meaning: the scornful exclamation used when something will never happen, like 'fat chance!'
A boy's name used in Arabic-speaking and Muslim countries

explanation.definitionFit: The two-word scoffing retort means 'no chance', and run together it spells a male Arabic given name.

clue.text: One making tears in jumper, épée waving around

indicators.note: around means the letters found there are turned round and read backwards
in tells the solver the answer sits inside the run of clue words that follows

explanation.surface: A fencer's sword, swung about carelessly, rips holes in a sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' picks REPEEW from the end of 'jumper', all of 'épée' and the start of 'waving'; 'around' turns it backwards. 'One making tears' looks like a ripper, but the tears are crying.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cries sheds tears, so a crier is literally one producing them.

clue.text: Create unopened wine without tax breaks

indicators.note: breaks means the second group of letters bursts into the middle of the first
unopened means the word for wine loses its first letter, as if its top were never removed

parts.note: vine is a stand-in for wine, the plant that yields it
without means having no, so no
VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax

explanation.surface: A sober instruction to produce something with no bottle opened and no duty paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unopened' leaves INE, and 'breaks' splits it open; 'Create' is a verb, so the answer is one too.
explanation.definitionFit: To innovate is to bring in something new, to devise and originate, which is a way of creating.

clue.text: Like a fish eating object with derision

indicators.note: eating means the word for fishlike takes the other word into its middle

parts.note: a fish is covered in scales, so it is scaly
an object is a thing

explanation.surface: A fish swallows some object, and someone watching mocks it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eating' signals the insertion; 'Like a fish' reads as a simile, but it is an adjective describing fish skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking scathingly means with withering scorn, which is the same as speaking with derision.

clue.text: See 16
Sing works by composer, a beat pioneer

indicators.note: works means the letters of the word beside it are worked over into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer

explanation.surface: A singer performs pieces by a composer who led a musical revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' gives GINS. 'beat' looks musical beside the singing and composer, but it is the Beat Generation of 1950s American writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Allen Ginsberg, author of Howl, was a founding poet of the Beat Generation of American writers.

clue.text: Huge figure of Russian writer seizing doughnut

indicators.note: seizing means the writer's name grabs the ring-shaped letter and holds it inside

parts.note: Nikolai Gogol wrote Dead Souls
a ring doughnut is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A huge Russian author grabs a doughnut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seizing' puts O inside GOGOL, after GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The number ten to the power of one hundred is a famously enormous figure, named by a child in 1938.

clue.text: It's good to drink case of claret in the neighbourhood houses

indicators.note: houses means the word for near holds the casing letters inside it

parts.note: something in the neighbourhood is near

indicators.note: case of means the outer letters of the next word, its casing

explanation.surface: A wine merchant's chatter about good claret stocked by local houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case of' takes C and T, the outer letters of 'claret'; 'houses' puts them inside NEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The drink of the gods in myth, and any delicious drink, is good to drink by description.

clue.text: Restaurant employee has red face, lacking good service

parts.note: Che Guevara, the revolutionary, was a red, a communist

indicators.note: lacking means the word face goes without the letters for the tennis term

parts.note: an ace is a winning serve in tennis

explanation.surface: A flushed waiter gives poor service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' takes ACE out of FACE, leaving F.
explanation.definitionFit: A cook running a restaurant kitchen is one of the people who work there.

clue.text: American's ball on right-winger's head

parts.note: a prom is an American school dance
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party, on the right

explanation.surface: An American school dance lands on the head of a conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' reads as a body part, but it is a headland jutting into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A head in geography is a headland, a high point of land jutting out into the sea.

clue.text: On which you might be called 'b___ cow'

definitions.text: On which you might be called

parts.note: the b standing in front of the blank is taken as written
to cow is to intimidate, also to lower or lour, to scowl menacingly

explanation.surface: Someone is rudely called a 'b___ cow' during a heated conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank invites a swear word, but the b is just a letter and 'cow' is a verb. A blower is British slang for the telephone.
explanation.definitionFit: Blower is British slang for a telephone, the device on which people are rung up.

clue.text: Wept with repair getting bodged — bugger!

indicators.note: a bodged job is clumsily botched, so these letters are muddled up

explanation.surface: Someone cries over a botched repair and swears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bugger' looks like an oath, but it means one who bugs, planting listening devices.
explanation.definitionFit: A bugger here is one who plants listening devices, which is what someone tapping a phone line does.

clue.text: Addresses with no food supplies

parts.note: O stands for nought, the figure zero, so none
rations are allotted food supplies

explanation.surface: Speeches delivered while the food has run out.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal speeches are addresses, as in an address to the nation.

clue.text: He generates huge interest seizing power — Richard III?

indicators.note: seizing means the moneylender's word grabs the letter for power

parts.note: a usurer lends money at exorbitant interest
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A greedy moneylender grabs power, like a notorious English king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interest' sounds like fascination, but it is the charge on a loan. The question mark marks Richard III as an example; historians dispute whether he seized the throne unlawfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard III took the English throne from his nephew, and so is often cited as someone who grabbed the crown unlawfully.

clue.text: Heroine meets dashing man, no cruel foreign bigwig

parts.note: Emma is the heroine of Jane Austen's novel

indicators.note: dashing means the letters rush around into a new order

explanation.surface: A romantic heroine meets a dashing, gentle man of importance from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dashing' rearranges MAN NO CRUEL to NUEL MACRON. 'dashing' looks like a compliment to the man, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmanuel Macron is the President of France, a powerful figure from a country other than Britain.

clue.text: Get depressed around midnight in night attire

indicators.note: around means the phrase for being depressed wraps itself about the letter from the night

parts.note: to get depressed is to be down
the middle of the word night is the letter G

explanation.surface: Someone feels low in the small hours, still in nightclothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'midnight' gives G, the middle letter of 'night'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedgown is a nightdress or nightgown, worn in bed and so a piece of nightwear.

clue.text: Strolled in centre of Bordeaux clad in pale colour

indicators.note: clad in means the middle letters are dressed in the outer words, sitting inside them

parts.note: wan means pale
red is a colour

indicators.note: centre of means the two middle letters of the city's name

explanation.surface: A walker in the heart of Bordeaux is dressed in a pale shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes the two middle letters of an eight-letter name; 'clad in' wraps the pale colour round them.
explanation.definitionFit: To wander is to roam or amble without hurry, much like taking a stroll.

clue.text: Note revolving musical boxes still

indicators.note: boxes means the turned title encloses the note
revolving means the musical's title turns round and is read backwards

parts.note: Cats is the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical
ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A note going round inside music boxes, yet still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolving' gives STAC, which 'boxes' the note.
explanation.definitionFit: Something static is motionless, not moving at all, which is a meaning of still.

clue.text: Coax to follow criminal offence in court

indicators.note: to follow means the word for coaxing comes after the word for criminal

parts.note: a con is a convict, a criminal
to coax someone is to tempt them

explanation.surface: Persuading a crook to commit an offence that lands in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offence in court' is contempt of court, disrespect to a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: Contempt of court, disobeying or disrespecting a court, is a legal offence.

clue.text: King in robe twirling about

indicators.note: twirling means the robe's letters spin into a new order

parts.note: on can mean about, as in a talk on art

explanation.surface: A monarch twirls about in his robe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twirling' rearranges ROBE to OBER.
explanation.definitionFit: Oberon is the king of the fairies in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Poke fun at an American state

parts.note: to guy someone is to mock or ridicule them

explanation.surface: Mocking one of the states of the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American state' reads as one of the fifty, but 'American' gives A and 'state' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Guyana is a country on the north coast of South America, an independent nation.

clue.text: Clever opening of golf range

parts.note: G is golf in the radio alphabet
ambit means scope or range

explanation.surface: A smart start at the golf driving range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' suggests a golf driving range, but it means scope.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambit is an opening move in chess that gives up a piece for advantage, so a crafty opening.

clue.text: Viewer who's turned on first of programmes with cat that's whizzing around

indicators.note: around means the word for urinating wraps itself about the opening letter

parts.note: to whizz is slang for to urinate, so whizzing is peeing

indicators.note: first of means the opening letter of the word programmes

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A viewer watching TV programmes with a cat racing round the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts P inside PEEING. 'whizzing' looks like speeding, but it is slang for urinating; 'turned on' means aroused.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyeur spies on people undressing for his own arousal, so is a watcher who is excited by it.

clue.text: Get diamonds for court favourite

parts.note: to get something is to see it, to understand
D is the abbreviation for the card suit diamonds

explanation.surface: Win jewels from a king's favourite at court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' looks royal, but it is a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis tournaments a seeded player is one ranked as likely to win, a favourite on court.

clue.text: Moments in a hearing of Congress

indicators.note: in a hearing of means the word that follows is heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: congress can mean sexual intercourse

explanation.surface: Short spells during a hearing held by the US Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' looks like the US legislature, but it means sexual intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Secs is short for seconds, which are brief moments of time.

clue.text: Old man and I picked up tar on the box

parts.note: pop is an informal name for father, one's old man

indicators.note: picked up means the letter I is caught by ear and written as the word that sounds the same

parts.note: the letter I said aloud is the word eye

explanation.surface: A father and I collected some tar from the box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tar' is a sailor, and 'the box' is television.
explanation.definitionFit: Popeye the Sailor is a cartoon seaman shown on television, so a sailor on TV.

clue.text: Left cutting piece of cake, I'm not sure this settles it

indicators.note: cutting means the letter for left slices into the word for something easy

parts.note: a cinch is something easy, a piece of cake
er is the sound of hesitation or doubt

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates over a slice of left-over cake, wondering if it decides the matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A clincher is a decisive argument or fact that ends a dispute once and for all.
